comments: I'm assuming `SelectMany()` and `Concat()` are just alternative names for the same proposed method? Why not just stick with one? I personally would prefer exposing `Concat()` as an overload, since F# uses the same name for [its equivalent method](https://fsharp.github.io/fsharp-core-docs/reference/fsharp-collections-seqmodule.html#concat).

Note that another way to write this code is to use the existing overload of `Concat`:

```c#
Command.NameInfo.OnlineAccounts = 
    Input.WebAddresses.Select(x => CreateWebAddress(x))
        .Concat(Input.EmailAddresses.Select(x => CreateEmailAddress(x)))
        .ToList();
```

Or:

```c#
Command.NameInfo.OnlineAccounts = Enumerable.Concat(
    Input.WebAddresses.Select(x => CreateWebAddress(x)),
    Input.EmailAddresses.Select(x => CreateEmailAddress(x))
).ToList();
```

But you do have to choose between the fluent assymetric form and the non-fluent symmetric form. So I think the proposed overload of `Concat` would still be a good addition.
Agreed, @TonyValenti if you could update the OP following the API proposal template we can consider this proposal for .NET 7.

review_comments:
I was fairly split about what approach to follow here. Ultimately I went with modifying the implementation for a couple of reasons:

1. It doesn't fundamentally change the implementation characteristics of the existing Concat methods.
2. It avoids creating a linked list of nested concat iterators: this means reduced allocations plus it avoids _O(k^2)_ iteration of _k_ concatenated enumerables. In most applications that _k_ is constant though.

This will null ref if source yields a null element.  Is that the desired behavior?  That does appear to be consistent with at least a few other places I audited, e.g. SelectMany, but wanted to double-check.

Yes, I picked this up from the `SelectMany` implementation. I think this is the desired behavior, throwing `ArgumentNullException` should be reserved for `IEnumerable<T>` construction, doing it during enumeration seems inappropriate to me.

Did you consider just doing:
```C#
return sources.SelectMany(e => e);
```
rather than implementing another iterator?

I did, ultimately it's tradeoff between this and a closure allocation and a few virtual calls. I should point out that the simple `SelectMany` implementation does inherit from `Iterator<T>`, but ultimately I didn't find any of the speed optimizations offered in this particular case to be useful in practice.

> I did, ultimately it's tradeoff between this and a closure allocation and a few virtual calls

There's no closure allocation with `sources.SelectMany(e => e)`.  There is one delegate per T allocated for the process.  And an extra delegate invocation per enumerable.  From my perspective, I'd rather have less code to maintain and a smaller binary (and implicitly pick up any optimizations SelectMany adds in the future, e.g. if it were to special case T[]).  Up to you, though.

The whole purpose of this API is to allow someone to write:
```C#
a.Concat(b, c, d);
```
rather than:
```C#
a.Concat(b).Concat(c).Concat(d);
```
?  That doesn't seem worthwhile, in my opinion.
I think there are arguments to be made about terseness and discoverability. It also allows concatenating arbitrarily many enumerables without needing to foreach over the inputs.

>  It also allows concatenating arbitrarily many enumerables without needing to foreach over the inputs

That's what Flatten does.  This would only be used if you had two individual enumerables and an array of enumerables. That can't be common.

It's slightly different than Flatten in that the number of flattened segments can be known ahead of enumeration, plus the optimizations applied by Concat's `Iterator<T>` implementation. I agree about the signature being awkward for this type of use. 

I still think `a.Concat(b,c,d)` is an improvement over `a.Concat(b).Concat(c).Concat(d)`.

> It's slightly different than Flatten in that the number of flattened segments can be known ahead of enumeration

It can with Flatten as well, with TryGetNonEnumeratedCount.  That will benefit more than just arrays as well.

> I agree about the signature being awkward for this type of use.

More than awkward, I don't see it being used at all for that kind of use.  That would mean I have an `IEnumerable<T>[] source` and I write code like:
```C#
return source.Length switch
{
    0 => Enumerable.Empty<T>(),
    1 => source[0],
    2 => source[0].Concat(source[1]),
    _ => source[0].Concat(source[1], source[2..]),
}
```
which I don't imagine anyone will do.

That means the only reason this is being added is to be able to write:
```C#
a.Concat(b, c, d);
```
instead of:
```C#
a.Concat(b).Concat(c).Concat(d);
```
which, to me at least, is not worth it.  I understand it was already reviewed by others and folks agreed to add it, so it's up to you, but from a value perspective, I don't see this being worth a lot of code.

And if we do decide to keep it, FWIW I disagree with the separation of the second argument from the rest of the params.  Yes, it avoids someone writing the nop `e.Concat()`, but it also prevents someone from writing `a.Concat(array)` and instead forces them to slice that array to separate out the car and the cdr.  If we're going through the effort now and in the future to have this overload, I'd say the utility of supporting the array is more beneficial than preventing someone from writing `e.Concat()`.  There are many other mostly useless things folks can write with LINQ already that we don't prevent, e.g. `e.Select(i => i)`, `e.Where(i => true)`, etc.  To me, that's a job for an analyzer if we want to tell people that are doing things that aren't actually useful, ala https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/33770.

> That means the only reason this is being added is to be able to write:

There's also the theoretical performance improvement of avoiding a linked-list representation of the iterator cf. https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/61230#discussion_r743579004

> FWIW I disagree with the separation of the second argument from the rest of the params.

Ultimately it's tradeoff between allowing `a.Concat()` and making `a.Concat(array)` possible. This wouldn't prevent slicing in your example though, you'd still have to write `source[0].Concat(source[1..])`

> Ultimately it's tradeoff between allowing a.Concat() and making a.Concat(array) possible

Right. Why is the former deemed more negatively impactful than the latter is beneficial?

> This wouldn't prevent slicing in your example though

It would if I had a single enumerable and wanted to concat an array I get from somewhere. The current signature requires me to get _two_ single enumerables from somewhere plus that array.  In other words, I already have an enumerable I'm using LINQ to construct: if I get an array of enumerables from somewhere, I just concat that on, but with this signature, I need to split that incoming array.

Do we have concrete use examples for these APIs? Examples from around GitHub, etc.?  I'm curious what we used to drive the addition of these methods.

> Right. Why is the former deemed more negatively impactful than the latter is beneficial?

That just happened to be the prevailing opinion during API review. Would you like us to review it again?
I don't agree with the tradeoff.  But if all aspects of it were appropriately discussed and the overall opinion was this was the best tradeoff, ok.  I still question the API all-up, but, yeah.
